turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): In you come, Hannah. Lorraine, grab that seat. We'll get the dressing sorted in a minute.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): We've been out there nearly forty minutes. I'm wrecked, and the bub still needs a feed.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'm Lorraine, the carer. I've been living in with her since she got home from the caesar.
[SEG0004] person_4 (DOCTOR): Sorry, this computer's crawling. What brings you in today?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): The wound from the caesarean. Ten days ago. It's gone red and there's gunk leaking out.
[SEG0006] person_4 (DOCTOR): Say that again? I had the wrong file up.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Caesar. Ten days back. The cut's red and it's leaking. I'm over it, honestly.
[SEG0008] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And she was really hot last night.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): When did the redness start?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, a couple of days, I think it was—
[SEG0011] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Sorry, the pram's half across the doorway. Some bloke nearly went over it. Go on, love.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Two days. I saw it two days ago.
[SEG0013] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It was already red on Saturday in the shower. That's four days, not two.
[SEG0014] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right, so roughly two to four days, I won't lock it in. When did the discharge start?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Yesterday arvo. Yellow sticky stuff on the pad.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): Was the fever just last night, or today as well?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose I felt a bit warm this morning. Not really, though.
[SEG0018] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Home thermometer was thirty-eight point four last night. She looked miserable under the doona.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any shivers or shaking with that?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I wasn't shivering.
[SEG0021] person_3 (CAREGIVER): You were, Hannah. You were shaking at midnight. I went and got another blanket.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): I was cold and tired. That is not shivering.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): Is the wound sore?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Really sore if I stand up or pick the bub up. Panadol takes the edge off.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): Is that pain getting worse each day?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometimes, not really. Mm, I suppose.
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any smell from it?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose... not really. I can't tell, my nose is hopeless.
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any vomiting?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I'm not running to the loo either. Bowels are just a bit slow, nothing mad.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): Stinging when you wee?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Waterworks are fine.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): Cough, phlegm, any chest symptoms?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough. Chest is fine.
[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any medicine allergies?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): What are you taking?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Panadol, the little red iron tablets, and I was on those Flopen capsules.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): How many days of the Flopen did you do?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Five days... or was it seven? I stopped when the packet looked finished. I think.
[SEG0041] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Hospital said seven days. She slept through a couple, so I doubt she got every dose.
[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): What's the dose? The discharge letter still hasn't loaded.
[SEG0043] person_1 (NURSE): It's up. Flucloxacillin 500 mg, four times a day, for seven days, from the day she left.
[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): The iron tablets?
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): One red iron tablet every morning, for the low iron. Been on them since I was pregnant.
[SEG0046] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yes, iron deficiency is on your file. Keep those going.
[SEG0047] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She had the belly needles as well, the Clexane. Last one was yesterday morning.
[SEG0048] person_1 (NURSE): The chart says enoxaparin 40 mg once a day.
[SEG0049] person_3 (CAREGIVER): No. The syringes in the fridge were 20 mg, the smaller ones. I read the barrel every time.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): I never looked at them. Can we just get to the wound?
[SEG0051] person_4 (DOCTOR): How much Panadol?
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Two tablets, four times a day. I swallow them. I miss the lunchtime one if I crash out.
[SEG0053] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any Nurofen or ibuprofen?
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah nah. Nurofen wrecks my stomach. I never took it.
[SEG0055] person_1 (NURSE): Dressing's coming down. It might tug.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Ow. Yeah, it's stuck. Just rip it off.
[SEG0057] person_1 (NURSE): Lower end of the caesarean wound is red for about three centimetres, skin's warm, yellow discharge on the gauze. The edges are still together, it's not gaping.
[SEG0058] person_4 (DOCTOR): Again, Brooke? I clicked the wrong window.
[SEG0059] person_1 (NURSE): Redness about three centimetres at the lower end, warm skin, yellow discharge, edges intact.
[SEG0060] person_4 (DOCTOR): Tender if I press here?
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Don't. That's the sore bit.
[SEG0062] person_1 (NURSE): Obs. Temperature 37.3, heart rate 96, blood pressure 138 over 84, oxygen sats 98 percent, respiratory rate 18.
[SEG0063] person_4 (DOCTOR): This is a wound infection, I think. Superficial for now. That's a working impression, not proven till we get a result.
[SEG0064] person_4 (DOCTOR): I want a swab of the discharge sent to the lab today, before you start a new antibiotic.
[SEG0065] person_1 (NURSE): I'll take the swab on the way out.
[SEG0066] person_4 (DOCTOR): For the wound infection I'm switching you to Augmentin Duo Forte, 875 over 125, one tablet by mouth twice a day for five days.
[SEG0067] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's breastfeeding the bub. Is Augmentin alright with that?
[SEG0068] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yes. Augmentin is fine while you're breastfeeding. Take it with food so it sits better.
[SEG0069] person_4 (DOCTOR): Keep the wound clean and dry, fresh dressing only. No creams, and no Dettol on it.
[SEG0070] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. I just want to go home.
[SEG0071] person_4 (DOCTOR): If you get a high fever, the redness spreads quickly, or you feel faint, go to emergency. Don't wait.
[SEG0072] person_4 (DOCTOR): Otherwise I'll see you back in this clinic in two days.
[SEG0073] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Two days. And if it's worse by then, not better?
[SEG0074] person_4 (DOCTOR): If it's worse in two days I might organise an ultrasound of the wound. Not today.
[SEG0075] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. Can we leave? I'm wrecked and the car park will be a nightmare.
[SEG0076] person_1 (NURSE): Fresh dressing, then the swab, then you're done. Nearly there, Hannah.

spec.situation: Patient 10 days after a hernia, appendix or caesarean operation; wound redness and discharge, fever the night before; nurse removes dressing and describes it; patient is vague about antibiotic course ('five days... or was it seven'); wound swab and antibiotic change.
features: interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats
